content: 1. A well-characterized panel of known positive and negative samples should be used for testing, which may include prospective parallel testing of the current gold standard and the new diagnostic test on clinical specimens. Verification studies are essential when commercial tests are used, ensuring they align with the manufacturer’s intended use. These studies typically involve blinded testing of a well-characterized panel of known positive and negative samples, adhering to national or international accreditation requirements. 2. Validation studies are a critical component of the WHO review process and the development of recommendations for the use of new diagnostic tests. Once large-scale validation studies are published and the target performance characteristics of a test are established, laboratories implementing the method do not need to repeat such large-scale studies. Instead, they must ensure the test is used as described in the validation studies and confirm its suitability for the intended patient population. 3. Countries must determine the need for verification based on their national guidelines and accreditation requirements. They should also complete national regulatory processes by collaborating with government authorities, manufacturers, and authorized service providers to meet the requirements of the national regulatory authority. Sufficient time must be allocated for submitting applications and providing supplementary evidence as needed. 4. Selecting, procuring, installing, and setting up appropriate equipment is a vital step in implementing a new diagnostic test. The choice of instruments should align with the needs of the clinical or microbiological laboratory and the intended use of the diagnostic test. Instruments should be widely available, supported by reliable manufacturer supply chains, and cost-effective. Where feasible, integrating tuberculosis (TB) testing into existing platforms should be prioritized to enhance cost-efficiency. In high TB workload settings, dedicated instruments may be preferred. Expert setup, often performed by the manufacturer’s engineers or authorized service providers, is generally required. Some automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) may necessitate infrastructure modifications to accommodate the instrumentation. 5. Instrument verification must be conducted before testing clinical specimens to ensure the equipment is fit for purpose. This involves testing with known positive and negative materials during installation, after servicing or calibration, or following instrument relocation. Preventive maintenance and ad hoc servicing are essential to maintain instrument performance. Regular maintenance should be performed by end-users, while suppliers or authorized service providers should handle on-request servicing. Extended warranties or service contracts should be utilized to ensure continued instrument functionality. 6. Testing sites must be assessed for readiness using standardized checklists before clinical specimen testing begins. Factors such as TB epidemiology, geographic considerations, testing workload, availability of qualified staff, referral network efficiency, and patient access to services should guide site selection. Existing sites should undergo regular assessments for safety and operational functionality. Functional testing sites require clean, secure, and suitable locations for instrument placement, with controlled environmental conditions such as humidity and temperature. WHO biosafety recommendations must be followed, including appropriate containment facilities, personal protective equipment, and safe disposal of biological waste. 7. Ensuring uninterrupted availability of reagents and disposables at testing sites is critical for maintaining technical capacity and consistent service delivery. Measures include involving qualified laboratory staff in defining specifications, streamlining importation and distribution procedures, monitoring consumption rates, tracking reagent shelf lives, and forecasting to avoid expirations or stock-outs. Proper planning is necessary to ensure training and equipment installation precede reagent shipments. Ongoing monitoring of procurement and supply chain steps is essential to minimize delays and ensure timely delivery of correct reagents. 8. Reagent quality and shelf life must be routinely monitored to ensure high-quality test results. Standard operating procedures (SOPs) for handling reagents and chemicals should be established to maintain quality and safety. Lot-to-lot verification testing should be performed on new batches of reagents or test kits, comparing results to existing materials with known performance. This testing may also monitor conditions during transport and storage within the country. WHO recommends using positive and negative controls for quality control (QC) when testing new reagent batches. 9. Comprehensive SOPs must be developed to address all aspects of the diagnostic testing process, from patient identification to result reporting and waste management. These SOPs should be readily available to staff and regularly updated. Clinical protocols and guidance are also necessary for selecting patients, ordering tests, interpreting results, and making patient-care decisions. Clinical staff must be informed and trained on planned changes before introducing new diagnostic tests or modifying existing ones. Monitoring the rate of test ordering ensures proper utilization, and additional training may be required for sites with low or unexpectedly high testing rates. 10. Digital data and diagnostic connectivity should be leveraged to enhance testing efficiency. Implementation plans should address software and hardware requirements to enable reliable data transmission and remote monitoring of performance, quality assurance (QA), and inventory management. Diagnostic connectivity allows for tracking consumption, identifying poor-performing instruments, and preemptively addressing issues to avoid instrument failure. This approach is cost-effective and supports reporting and integration with treatment sites. 11. A comprehensive QA program is essential to ensure the accuracy, reliability, and reproducibility of test results. Key elements include SOPs, training, competency assessment, instrument verification and maintenance, method validation, lot-to-lot testing, internal QC, external quality assessment (EQA), and continuous quality improvement. EQA programs involve proficiency testing, re-checking samples, inter-laboratory comparisons, on-site supervision, and timely feedback. Proficiency testing compares site results with reference results to identify deficiencies and evaluate user proficiency. Re-checking samples at higher-level laboratories provides external quality assessment. On-site supervisory visits should prioritize poorly performing sites identified through proficiency testing or performance monitoring. 12. Governance structures for EQA programs vary by country, with central-level coordination by ministries of health, national TB programs, or national TB reference laboratories. In some settings, activities may be decentralized to regional levels. Central authorities provide policies, guidance, and tools for standardized QA activities, while regional and district levels operationalize and supervise these activities. Data collected at testing sites are reviewed regionally and centrally to inform and update policies and procedures.
